speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Workplace stressors, such as increased work demands, evolving work processes and blurred work-life boundaries became more pronounced.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: When not adequately managed, we witnessed how these work stressors eroded employee productivity and motivation, and negatively affected workplace mental wellness.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It can be said that the pandemic marked a watershed moment in our fight for better workplace mental wellness.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The pandemic revealed cracks in our workplaces and gave employers the impetus to build organisational resilience.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is heartening that there are some employers in both the public and private sectors who have heeded the call to improve workplace mental wellness.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Let us build on this momentum to support employers.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: According to reports, this lower level of employer engagement is a result of cost constraints, lack of awareness of mental wellness resources and scepticism about the returns of workplace mental wellness interventions.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To enable our employers to overcome these barriers, I believe that the Government can step up its efforts to increase the awareness of mental health resources and support employers in implementing better workplace mental health policies and practices, especially for small- and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs).

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: First, I will lay out the economic case for better workplace mental wellness.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These benefits were echoed by many business leaders at the CNA Leadership Summit 2022, who underscored tangible returns like increased productivity and higher employee retention after investing in mental well-being interventions.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Making an economic case for mental wellness at the workplace is crucial when seeking support from investors, shareholders and Government agencies, especially when it comes to financing mental health support.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Hence, equipping employers with tools to measure outcomes of mental wellness investments, benchmarking with industry standards and recognition in the form of awards will help employers seek buy-in and support from stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A Company of Good in Singapore must take care of their people in the workplace.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, when NVPC recognises them with this award, this can create positive ripple effects for corporate action on their priorities.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Upon establishing the case for workplace mental wellness intervention, the natural question that follows is: how should we go about taking action?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In the following part of my speech, I will lay out a roadmap for implementing workplace mental wellness interventions.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Before I proceed further, I would like to extend my heartfelt thanks to members of the Young People's Action Party (YP) and the National University of Singapore (NUS) Health and Well-being team for their contributions to the following recommendations.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The first step in any organisation's mental wellness journey is to assess the state of their employees' mental health regularly.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This can be achieved using a workplace mental health assessment tool.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I must stress that the confidentiality of the results from each employee's mental health assessment should be upheld at all costs.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Employers should only receive an aggregated set of results to identify workplace stressors and track changes in overall workplace mental wellness over time.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: At present, employers can utilise the iWorkHealth tool, an online, self-administered psychosocial health assessment tool for companies and their employees.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It was developed by the Ministry of Manpower (MOM)'s Workplace Safety and Health (WSH) Institute, in partnership with the WSH Council, Institute of Mental Health (IMH), Changi General Hospital (CGH) and Health Promotion Board (HPB).

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The tool provides employees with a survey questionnaire that covers stress-related factors in the workplace including job demands, job control, job recognition, organisation culture and relationships with supervisors and co-workers.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Upon completing this survey, employers will receive an aggregated anonymised department and company report identifying key workplace stressors, extent of workplace stress and the overall state of the mental well-being of their employees.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Participating employees will receive individual reports on their mental well-being scores and workplace stressors.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To illustrate the usefulness of workplace mental health assessments, I would like to share a real-life case study that came up in my conversation with an employer.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: After completing the assessment, the employer received aggregated data that showed that teams with higher manager-to-staff ratios had higher stresses and anxiety levels compared to teams with lower manager-to-staff ratios.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With this information, the employer inferred that managers who have larger teams had fewer opportunities to check in with their staff and offer mentorship and support.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This might have translated into higher levels of stress and anxiety among their staff.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To address this issue, the employer proceeded to transition into a more hierarchical organisational structure that allowed for the formation of smaller teams, according to more clearly delineated management levels and job scopes.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With lower manager-to-staff ratios, this allowed for more intra-team engagement.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In the next round of workplace mental health assessment, the employer noted lower workplace stress and anxiety levels, suggesting the positive effects of the restructuring exercise.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This case study highlights the value of the data gathered from workplace mental health assessments.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As illustrated, the data can direct recalibration of company policies and structures and concretely improve workplace mental wellness.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: At this point, I would like to ask the Minister for Manpower for an update on the iWorkHealth tool since its implementation.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Additionally, what other plans does the Ministry have to enhance the effectiveness and capabilities of the tool?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To further signal the importance of workplace mental wellness assessments, I propose that Enterprise SG grants, such as the Enterprise Development Grant and the Productivity Solutions Grant, include a survey on employees' well-being before and after the implementation of a project to measure potential improvement of employees' wellness, in addition to employees' value-added gains.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This will ensure that any company transformation takes into account the human wellness element to ensure better sustainability of outcomes.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This also signals to employers the importance of well-being and that, in turn, goes hand-in-hand with any transformation.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We will also need to incentivise and recognise employers.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I propose that one way to incentivise adoption can be to acknowledge companies who have integrated it into their workflow at the Annual Occupational Safety and Health (OSH) awards hosted by the Ministry of Manpower (MOM).

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As a proactive intervention, the workplace mental health assessment aligns with the wider Healthier SG strategy of preventive healthcare.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Proactive mental health interventions have been proven to generate a higher return on investments compared to reactive mental health interventions.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Other proactive mental health interventions, like awareness training and managers' training, also generated high returns of £5.3 and £6 respectively for every £1 invested.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In contrast, reactive mental health interventions, like workplace counselling for employees generated lower returns of £3.1 for every £1 invested.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Upon assessing the mental health of employees and identifying workplace stressors, the next step is for employers to develop a strategy to support employees' mental well-being.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is important for employers to go beyond a single programme to combat workplace mental health issues, since the positive effects of these initiatives are often limited to the objectives of that programme.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Instead, a workplace mental health integrated strategy can synchronise efforts across the organisation.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This results in a more unified, holistic, structured and sustainable approach towards improving workplace mental health.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: An example of a comprehensive and pioneering workplace mental health strategy that other organisations can take inspiration from is the WellNUS Workplace Mental Health Framework, designed by the Health and Well-being team at NUS.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The WellNUS Workplace Mental Health Framework systematically maps out the different parts of an employee's well-being journey and identifies the key relevant initiatives and key stakeholders to provide support.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The framework aims to support employees at every stage along the mental health spectrum from well states to states that may benefit from intervention and to recovery and back-to-work transition stages.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Presently, the WSH Council has launched a playbook on workplace mental well-being.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It provides employers with a guide on how to devise their own workplace mental wellness strategy by breaking it down into outcomes, targets and how-tos.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, there is room for it to be more robust, by considering mental well-being along a spectrum and proposing interventions that target different states of mental health.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In addition, interventions that can be undertaken by different levels of staff, senior leaders, human resources (HR), Occupational Safety and Health (OSH) and so on, and of different natures – culture and strategy, systems, infrastructure, support services and resources – should be included as well.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Once a mental wellness strategy has been devised, interventions can then be implemented.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But the question that follows is	– who will be tasked to put these interventions into place?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While establishing a health and wellness team might not always be a viable solution for SMEs with leaner teams and tighter wellness budgets, a cost-effective alternative can be to broaden the job scope of current HR managers, teams or other relevant managers to include workplace mental well-being.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Incorporating well-being interventions into HR systems signals that mental health is not a tangential concern but an organisational priority.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Such a reframing of mental wellness in the workplace is necessary for real change to happen.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I must emphasise that reconceptualising the role of HR is not meant to increase the workload of our already saturated HR managers.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Instead, it is to bring our HR systems up to speed with the growing needs of our workforce.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Hence, it would be helpful to arrive at a collective definition of the additional skillsets required of HR teams or relevant personnel to support workplace mental well-being.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Based on our consultations with existing well-being managers, these skillsets include knowledge in organisational psychology, corporate policy development and designing evidence-based health and well-being corporate programmes.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Given the specificity and interdisciplinary nature of skillsets required to support workplace mental well-being, there is a shortage of people who can fill these positions and we need to do more to bridge this skills gap.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Before I proceed with my recommendations on bridging the skills gap, I acknowledge that not all companies have the capacity to upskill their HR managers or incorporate new responsibilities into their job scopes.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This might be more prevalent in micro enterprises.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In such cases, can we think of outsourcing this work to a central intermediary so that more similarly sized companies can lean on it?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For larger SMEs, would a tax incentive be enough to upskill relevant individuals in the company?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Such measures are necessary to bring all our SMEs up to speed rather than only those who can afford mental wellness interventions.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These courses can be introduced in a tiered fashion, with tier 1 being peer support training, directed at all employees and Tier 2 being managerial training, directed at those in leadership positions, with more extensive structural discussions on organisational structure and workplace culture.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: During peer support training, employees can be trained to notice distress signals from colleagues, direct colleagues to the appropriate mental health services and resources and provide psychological first aid.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The NUS Health and Well-being team, for instance, has launched an NUS Peer Support System that provides a two-day training programme for peer supporters.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: After the training, NUS peer supporters meet quarterly to check in with one another.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They will also be given the opportunity to participate in elective modules to refresh and enhance their peer support skills.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Managerial training should encompass peer support training in addition to other aspects that capitalise on managers' proximity and frequency of interactions with employees.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Managerial training can include more in-depth discussions on organisational structure, shaping a mentally healthy workplace culture and cultivating stronger networks of connection between a manager and the staff.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: After training, there should be regular check-ins and a framework as well so that there is follow-through for the training provided.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A notable example is the Young NTUC WSQ-certified training in peer-to-peer mental wellbeing support at workplaces.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Learning circles comprising individuals who have completed the peer-to-peer training serve as a regular check-in and forum to share lived experiences and best practices at various workplaces.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A suggestion to expand on our call for managerial training is to create specific modules for SME business owners.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Such modules take into account the unique context of SMEs and work closely with trade associations to curate the course content and co-delivery.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As it is often said, "it is lonely at the top." SME employers can feel isolated.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Hence, working with trade associations on the co-delivery of such training programmes can also create organic opportunities where employers provide employer-peer support and check-ins.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Even with frameworks and training programmes, some employers and managers might still require more customised and sustained guidance when implementing mental wellness interventions.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: One possible solution might be for Employee Assistance Programme (EAP) providers to go beyond counselling services and include consultancy services for employers and managers.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Consultancy resources are especially crucial for SMEs that might still be building up their health and well-being capabilities.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To harness economies of scale and build depth of services, Government funding can be channelled to a smaller pool of organisations instead of being spread more thinly across multiple EAP providers.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The normalisation of workplace mental wellness struggles has catalysed a shift in company cultures and employers' perceptions surrounding mental well-being.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We are now presented with a golden opportunity which will determine the state of workplace mental wellness in the future.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Hence, we need to be intentional in entrenching mental wellness as an organisational priority and sustaining growing wellness policies and programmes.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In this Motion, I have laid out six key processes to achieve these goals.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Let us walk this journey together and empower them.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: So, I will be precise in the reply.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: First of all, I thank the Member Edward Chia for his continued passion and interest in driving mental health and wellness at the workplace.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Within the taskforce, I lead a sub-group that looks specifically at improving employment and employability of persons with mental health conditions as well as strengthening support for mental well-being at the workplace.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We have just completed a series of public consultations on ideas that we are exploring.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: These include having trained mental health champions at the workplace, raising awareness and adoption of mental well-being resources available and reducing the stigma around mental health.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We will take into consideration the Member's inputs as we put together recommendations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: I also thank the Member for laying out the economic case for better workplace mental wellness.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: With the pandemic bringing mental health to the fore and the Government's support through several resources, many employers have started to put in place more measures to support their employees' mental well-being.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The Public Service Division has taken the lead by launching a suite of initiatives to better support our public officers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: These initiatives include having a whole-of-Government hotline for confidential counselling services to provide all our public officers a safe channel to speak to trained counsellors and building a community of Wellness Ambassadors to serve as added support at the workplace.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: As the Member has rightly pointed out, more can be done for workplaces in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: I echo the Member's suggestion for more companies to regularly assess the state of their employees' mental health, for example, through the use of the iWorkHealth (iWH) tool.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: It is a free online psychosocial tool for organisations and their employees.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: This is the first step to identifying psychosocial risks in the workplace by giving an indication on the state of mental well-being within the organisation, not just in areas with potential to cause risks but also in areas where the organisation has done well.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The customised and anonymised company report allows each participating company to have a better understanding of their employees' state of mental well-being and stress factors at work, which then allows them to implement targeted interventions to address the unique challenges of their company.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Since the tool was introduced in 2021, the Workplace Safety and Health (WSH) Council has been promoting the use of iWorkHealth through the trade associations and our tripartite partners.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Several Government agencies have also started using it.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: As of end-2022, more than 22,000 employees have used iWorkHealth.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: To encourage greater adoption, companies which adopt the iWorkHealth tool are awarded bonus points that count towards their overall standing to qualify for and win the bizSAFE Exemplary Awards.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Similarly, for the annual WSH CARE (Culture of Acceptance, Respect and Empathy) Awards, the use of iWorkHealth or any equivalent tool to regularly assess the state of workforce mental well-being will be a key criterion from this year onwards.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: To get more companies to embrace taking care of their employees as a priority, I believe that the National Volunteer and Philanthropy Centre (NVPC) will be happy to consider the Member's suggestion to include workplace mental health and well-being support in the new framework around corporate purpose for the recently launched new Company of Good programme.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: On workplace mental health competencies, I agree that the management, HR, supervisors and employees themselves can be better trained to support mental well-being at the workplace.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: In particular, HR plays a pivotal role in developing mental well-being policies and encouraging workers to go for mental well-being workshops to raise awareness and competencies.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Ideally, all workplaces should identify and equip relevant representatives to spot signs of mental distress and common mental health conditions, provide initial support to their co-workers and guide the person in distress to seek professional help.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Employers and those interested may wish to refer to the iWorkHealth website for a holistic framework which contains different types and levels of interventions and develop a strategy with interventions that best suit their own context.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: To support SMEs in strengthening their workplace mental well-being, we have the Total WSH Programme by the WSH Council.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: This programme provides free access to qualified consultants who can advise SMEs on how to manage safety and health in an integrated way and free intervention programmes such as mental well-being workshops to enhance SMEs' current support.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Similarly, HPB has a Workplace Outreach Wellness (WOW) package which supports both SMEs and large companies in rolling out broad-based workplace health programmes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: This includes mental health workshops and Workplace Health Programmes based on the company's readiness and their employees' needs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Training providers are able to contextualise these courses to suit the needs of the organisation, including the SMEs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Much has been said about what employers and HR can do to create more supportive workplaces.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We must not forget that workers too, have to take ownership of their mental well-being by taking active steps to stay positive mentally and to seek help when needed.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: This is similar to how each of us needs to take care of our physical health by having a balanced diet, adequate rest, exercise and seeking treatment when we fall ill.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Colleagues at the workplace can play a role as well, by providing emotional support to their peers or simply showing kindness and lending a listening ear to those around them.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Let us continue working together to build inclusive workplaces where workers can thrive in, and as part of our contribution to making Singapore a more inclusive place for all.
